cards.headline:
Virtual cell models get
a calibration framework
cards.body: Metrics like mean squared error often misjudge AI virtual cell models, so the authors propose a calibration framework.
cards.source: GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News

blocks.x: Published in Nature Biotechnology, the paper “Deep Learning Perturbation Models Can Outperform Baselines on Calibrated Metrics” introduces a positive-control baseline and a framework for testing whether common metrics can distinguish meaningful model predictions from less informative ones.

Genetic perturbation models, a subset of AI virtual cells, predict how activating or inhibiting genes alters a cell's transcriptome. Recent studies found sophisticated deep learning systems often failed to beat simple baselines.

The team built an “interpolated duplicate” positive control and the dynamic range fraction (DRF), which measures how well a metric separates it from a negative control. Across 14 datasets and 18 metrics, mean squared error and control-referenced Pearson correlation were often poorly calibrated; weighted and rank-based metrics such as WMSE, weighted RΔ2 and NIR were better.

On calibrated metrics, earlier models including scGPT and GEARS often surpassed uninformative baselines, and PRESAGE and scLambda performed more strongly. In Norman19 (0.63% of gene combinations covered) an additive baseline stayed hard to beat; in Wessels23 (10.3%) several models beat it.
Shift Bioscience, based in Cambridge, U.K., plans to apply the framework to screens for targets relevant to rejuvenation and age-related disease, initially focusing on fibrosis.
